text:
Recent work supports probing temporal dependence, but unrestricted shuffling has interpretive limits. [Does It Look Sequential? (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.12008) compares original and shuffled histories across 15 datasets, finding weak sequential structure in several popular benchmarks. [IDEA (SIGIR 2025)](https://le-wu.com/files/Publications/CONFERENCES/SIGIR25-IDEA.pdf) highlights distribution shifts and warns that arbitrary augmentations can discard informative interactions or preserve noise. Together, these motivate a distinction: sensitivity to perturbed histories alone does not establish useful temporal reasoning; perturbations may also change history plausibility.

The statistical foundation is older: [Berrett et al.’s conditional permutation test](https://academic.oup.com/jrsssb/article/82/1/175/7056014) samples nonuniform permutations that preserve dependence on observed confounders; calibration depends on the estimated conditional distribution. A proposed adaptation—not an established recommendation-specific test—is to match training-history replacements on prefix length, item-frequency bins, title/description similarity and repetition, then compare local swaps at different distances from the final interaction. Report matching coverage, covariate imbalance, transition-support rates and paired target-rank/top-10 changes, stratified by perturbation distance and support. Preserve padding and optionally fix the latest item to isolate earlier-order effects. Treat these as descriptive sensitivity diagnostics unless conditional sampling assumptions justify formal p-values; neither matching nor rank changes establish causality. Reuse one frozen NextItNet per category, derive matches only from public training data, and keep diagnostic results separate from pinned macro validation HR@10. The located sources do not establish this exact matched-history protocol as a standard 2024–2026 method.
